In contexts where there are disproportionate amounts of class-balanced data, a simple yet efficient nearest-neighbor classification technique relies on the principle that nearby points tend to belong to the same class. However, when dealing with severely unbalanced data, the near-optimal nearest-neighbor classifier often falls short due to an overemphasis on the minority class. A novel approach aims to rectify this by implementing a weighted classification method, where proximity weights are assigned according to the class's relative abundance. This allows for an adaptive balance between detecting minority-class observations and achieving higher overall classification accuracies. A comprehensive comparison between this proposed statistical approach and other existing techniques is conducted, showcasing its robustness and superiority, particularly in the face of complex datasets. Furthermore, a simple expectation-maximization algorithm is developed to seamlessly determine the proximity weights from a kernel matrix obtained through kernel partial least squares, thereby streamlining the process of optimizing these weights. Ultimately, the efficacy of the proposed technique is demonstrated through its successful handling of two large, high-dimensional datasets characterized by near-balanced distributions of classes, where it significantly outperformed conventional methods. Recent years have witnessed significant interest in the contraction theory of standard forms for entropic shocks and rarefaction waves within the framework of systems of conservation laws. This interest stems from its potential in developing efficient and straightforward numerical methods, particularly those without a limit in spatial accuracy, to accurately solve conservation law problems. Though the theory is well-established, it is primarily applied to specific standard forms rather than the general class, which also requires the establishment of a method to determine initial conditions for rarefaction waves, and to handle cases where a unique solution does not exist. This paper aims to address these gaps and outlines specific procedures for shocks and rarefaction waves, effectively proving the existence and uniqueness of initial values for rarefaction waves and demonstrating the possibility of cases without solution uniqueness. Furthermore, numerical methods based on the proposed framework are shown to be effective, including for cases without solution uniqueness and standard forms with multiple conserved vectors. Additionally, methods to handle multiple conserved vectors and the issue of vanishing mean-oxygen solution are discussed. Lastly, theoretical results are validated through numerical examples in two-dimensional flow around a cylinder problems. Estimates suggest that error rates are generally first-order, except for cases with standard forms in a specific form derived from the Riemann invariants or the entropic cone, which can exhibit second-order accuracy. Nonetheless, theoretical second-order rates have yet to be confirmed. Numerical results for first-order methods demonstrate a high degree of accuracy and precision when implemented in multiple-conserved-vector cases and without solution uniqueness. Importantly, methods do not rely on knowledge of the solution and are therefore often valuable for problems that cannot be solved analytically, such as vanishing mean-oxygen solutions and multi-dimensional problems like flow around a cylinder. Numerical results reveal a high degree of accuracy for these more complex scenarios. Numerical methods have also been shown to be insensitive to the choice of conserved vectors, and it is anticipated that higher-order rates may be achieved in future work. [Abstract]

We explore novel view generation in computer vision through conditional diffusion models, which have shown success in image-to-image translation tasks. Our goal is to develop a model that can generate dynamic and plausible novel views from arbitrary given images. To address potential convergence issues in diffusion models, we integrate a temporal coherence constraint, enabling the model to retain memory of previous samples and produce consistent novel view generations across time. Experimental results confirm that our approach leads to novel view generations consistent with the original image and previous ones, surpassing state-of-the-art methods in visual quality and coherence. Notably, our approach outperforms existing novel view generation methods in both quantitative and qualitative evaluations. Our technique has been successfully applied in virtual augmented reality environments without prior knowledge or pre-trained models. A novel approach to modeling, optimization, and control of complex systems is based on a data-driven framework that utilizes a machine learning technique called dynamic graph neural networks (D-GNNs). This method employs graph neural networks (GNNs) to model dynamic processes by integrating current states, parameters, and external influences. Since D-GNNs rely solely on system data, they can be applied without prior process knowledge, making them suitable for a wide variety of complex systems. This work discusses a general D-GNN-based method for prediction, optimization, and control of networked systems, demonstrated with an application to the SIS epidemic model. Through simulation, the proposed approach is compared with existing linear methods. Additionally, a case study illustrating the D-GNN application to the SIS model is presented, showing its effectiveness in optimization and control scenarios. This research showcases the effectiveness of a data-driven approach for modeling, optimization, and control of complex dynamic networks and may contribute to advancing control theories for complex systems. This work was originally published in the journal Automatica and the original paper can be accessed at https://www.sciencedirect.com/scoriet/journals/automatica. All data and code used in this research can be obtained upon request to the author. The D-GNN framework itself is built upon the PINNCE package, which is publicly available at https://github.com/svosec/pince. Further information on the SIS epidemic model and its control can be found in the book by Meng et al., which is publicly available at https://www.amazon.com/Complex-Networks-Applications-Applications-Algorithms-Applications/dp/1498770719. The proposed optimization and control D-GNN approach is an original contribution of this research. The corresponding control D-GNN application, which uses reinforcement learning as opposed to the predictive approach used in the case study, was originally presented at the 2020 IEEE CDC conference in Barcelona, Spain. A related research on the D-GNN-based prediction, optimization, and control framework is presented in another work, which is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.11113. This research is an extension of three other publications, which are available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.46465, https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.04350, and https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.04352. The current work is an integration of three other research papers in the order of prediction, optimization, and control.

This combination of factors is thought to be the source of delayed instability, which is explored through mathematical modeling and comparisons with similar scenarios involving flowing fibers. We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation, specifically focusing on $\alpha$-dissipative solutions with $\alpha$ a constant in the interval $[0,1]$. We introduce and study a flow-like partial differential equation to explore Lipschitz stability; this involves initial data perturbations and an energy-enhancing function. By determining the well-posedness of this equation, we conclude that the set of $\alpha$-dissipative solutions forms a closed subset within the set of Lipschitz continuous solutions with the weak Lipschitz norm for $0 \leq \alpha \leq 1$. Furthermore, we find that this closedness result translates to the set of semiconvex solutions with the sup-norm for convex solutions where $0 < \alpha \lesssim 1$. We also investigate the stability behavior within the set of weakly dissipative solutions, showing that the solution at a fixed time can be approximated by the $\alpha$-dissipative solution for any $0 \leq \alpha \leq 1$ in a specific norm related to the energy and dissipation. By using the stability at a fixed time, we extend the result to temporal weak Lipschitz stability for the Hunter-Saxton equation within the set of weakly dissipative solutions with a dissipation rate function for any $0 \leq \alpha \leq 1$. We further demonstrate that the temporal weak Lipschitz stability implies the well-posedness of a flow-like partial differential equation for any $0 \leq \alpha \leq 1$. This paper introduces a novel method for duration modification in speech synthesis, enabling either equalization or reversal of the original duration pattern. A key component of this method is the use of a non-parametric median-based strategy for data segmentation and outlier detection. Employing dynamic time warping distances, this approach aggregates short durations into unique, empirically-based classes for duration normalization. Subsequently, a technique called Iterative Imputation using a Multivariate Normal Voronoi Polytope has been adapted and integrated to address cases where no observations exist in a duration class, facilitating complete duration profile coverage. Experimental evaluations on two non-standard speech languages, Katibula and Ojibwa, demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in successfully modifying speech durations. Moreover, a subjective listener preference study reveals that the produced durations are perceived as more natural than those obtained using a widely regarded rule-based approach. Durations resulting from this method can serve as an useful preprocessing step for various tasks such as speech translation, cross-language speech synthesis, and durational normalization. Additionally, this method has been made available as an open-source repository on GitHub.

Advanced control strategies can unlock the full potential of industrial robots, outperforming the precision and consistency achieved with traditional position feedback methods. This study presents a cutting-edge trajectory following system for an industrial robot, incorporating secondary sensors located within the drive train to provide confidence intervals for actual joint positions. Leveraging this information, a novel flatness-based controller is designed to optimize performance, while the role of primary encoders in determining the secondary sensors' calibration is explored. Through a detailed theoretical analysis, the benefits of this approach are quantified, demonstrating improved robustness and convergence when faced with uncertainties in dynamic models, external disturbances, and errors in parameter estimation. Experimental results confirm that these advantages can be significantly increased by using flatness-based control with secondary encoders, achieving up to 10 times faster convergence compared to a more conservative control method. Furthermore, when the quality of primary encoders is comparable to that of accurate absolute encoders, the additional sensors offer little benefit, highlighting the need to consider the interplay between hardware and software components in industrial robot control systems. This research showcases an optimal configuration of the GRIP robot's last joint, achieving a steady-state positioning error below 1 micrometer after 1 second. This achievement demonstrates that upgrading existing industrial robots with low-cost secondary sensors can bring about affordable yet significant improvements in performance, with potential applications in a variety of robotic systems. Lastly, the principles underlying the presented methods can be adapted to a range of different configurations, encouraging further research into the design of optimal sensor combinations. This work has been formally reviewed and validated at Robotix, a leading French robotics company, and forms the basis of a patent application. The associated data and software can be accessed at https://git.lmt.org/FlatnessBasedRegulation.

The study of contingent life courses has gained significant interest across various disciplines. Multidimensional data that tracks individuals' health over time, especially when they experience multiple events like multiple myocardial infarctions, presents a challenge from an analytical perspective. In this study, we propose the Multiple State Examination model (MoSE) to examine myocardial infarction patients in a comprehensive manner. MoSE considers three key aspects: physical health levels, cumulative infarction risk, and social connections, modeled using a unified stochastic equation and a simultaneous likelihood estimation technique. Using data from the Framingham Heart Study, our findings highlight the importance of implementing a multidimensional approach to understand cardiovascular disease more accurately, particularly when addressing disparities in health among women and minority groups. Additionally, through individual prognostic diagnostics, our results show that early relationships between women and healthcare providers or male friends negatively impact their physical health and increased likelihood of experiencing another myocardial infusion. Finally, our findings emphasize the need for individualized prevention and treatment plans, emphasizing the importance of nurturing social connections in preventing a second heart attack and improving overall physical health for men and women, especially when they have younger siblings, which may reduce their likelihood of experiencing a second myocardial infarction. The proposed methodology can address a broad range of multidimensional data on life course health trajectories, offering opportunities for further research and development. Effective mesh-free numerical methods for simulating electro-chemical phenomena in complex geometries rely on a particular meshless potential reconstruction technique that treats the entire domain and its interfaces uniformly. However, applying this approach to bulk materials and surfaces separately results in a high computational cost due to a large number of required control points, usually with a minimum spacing of a few times the inter-electron distance. Therefore, an alternative strategy involving a dual-kernel approach with different kernel types for bulk and surface integrals has been developed. In this approach, a larger domain mesh is used for bulk computations and a smaller surface mesh is used for computations involving the various interfaces, utilizing a specific scaling factor for surface computations to account for long-range effects, while a multi-center exponential decay term ensures a smooth transition between the two domains. Additionally, this method preserves key properties of the original equations such as positive definiteness, and it has been successfully tested on various benchmark problems including Brownian motion on a surface and an electrostatic coupling between a bulk solution and a surface-dependent charge distribution. The results show that this method reduces computational costs without compromising on accuracy. Furthermore, additional success cases are described which highlight the capabilities of this method for simulating a wide variety of electro-chemical phenomena involving complex geometries and interfaces at atomic length scales. The presented implementation is available under MIT license as part of the open-source scientific framework Deduce. The framework is specifically designed for simulating electro-chemical and electrokinetic phenomena with a focus on mesh-free methods, automatic differentiation, and Bayesian inference techniques. The provided repository includes a comprehensive description of the used programming practices, as well as detailed documentation for an easy and quick setup of the simulations. Furthermore, based on this implementation an accompanying demonstration video is available, showcasing the capabilities of the presented multi-center integration technique in Deduce. The resulting twistor actions accurately replicate the original Lagrangians and help clarify the underlying field theories in these higher-dimensional spin-off theories. These twistor actions also facilitate the reconstruction of these theories in their original form, and help to interpret results from the literature that may have been obscure. In addition, we've broadened the applicability of the twistor formulation, making it applicable to Yang-Mills theory in general, not just self-dual theories. We've also generalized the twistor approach to theories with a non-self-dual Yang-Mills sector and constants. We've then applied these generalized twistor actions to investigate the properties of theories in even dimensions and the implications of their non-compact twistor actions for their time-like properties. The analysis reveals time-like properties that are analogous to those in the twistor actions for four-dimensional Yang-Mills theory and ten-dimensional self-dual Yang-Mills theory. Complications arise in other cases due to non-self-dual behavior in some of the twistor actions, which need to be addressed by incorporating a new type of twister action component, referred to as a "leg-over" field. The analysis then extends to theories in eleven dimensions, where the results reveal a non-manifestly Yang-Mills structure, but one that can be easily recovered with appropriate gauge fixing. Finally, we've outlined the potential applications of these twistor actions in eleven-dimensional Yang-Mills theory, such as further developing the recently proposed double field theory formulation. The analysis provides fresh insights into time-like properties in theories in even dimensions, as well as a foundation for exploring time-like behavior in eleven-dimensional Yang-Mills theory in a first-order, self-consistent formalism. The analysis includes an in-depth investigation of time-like effects in theories in eight, ten and eleven dimensions, as well as a comprehensive exploration of their non-linear properties, which have not been addressed in previous literature. The application of deep neural networks in medical image classification has shown great promise due to their advanced image mapping capabilities. Despite this, they are often plagued by the significant issue of label noise, which greatly affects their performance. Current methods aimed at reducing label noise typically rely on regularization techniques. In our research, we have developed a novel method known as the Bayesian Statistics-Guided Label Rejuvenation (BSGRL) that utilizes labeled data to modify the loss function and thereby decreases the impact of noisy labels. BSGGL works by leveraging Bayesian statistics principles to assign a probability value to each label, thereby differentiating noisy labels from high-confidence reliable labels. Through experimentation, we have found that BSGGL is effective against symmetric and asymmetric label noise, and outperforms existing noise reduction methods in some cases. Furthermore, we have successfully tested BSGGL on challenging datasets including Clean-Noise Mixup and the Colorectal Polyp dataset, and obtained promising results. Our research suggests that BSGGL is a robust and efficient solution for mitigating label noise in medical image classification tasks. The source code for BSGGL is available online at GitHub. Using a combination of numerical and analytical methods, we investigated the behavior of a lattice model of this type based on the minimal coupling of electrons to the magnetic field in a square planar lattice. We address the challenge of training a neural network (the student) to mimic an expert function, where the expert uses another network (the generator) to generate input values for its primary input. Specifically, the generator takes in latent codes and uses them to create domain-specific inputs that aid the expert in producing the final output. Prior approaches have relied on manual intervention to pre-synch the generator and student, but this can be impractical and limits the types of problems that can be tackled. We propose a novel, semi-supervised method that requires minimal human involvement, allowing the student to learn the input mapping on its own without the need for additional training data. We also introduce a new data enhancement technique, auto-optimization, which optimizes the distribution of domain-specific inputs generated by the generator to benefit the student. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method on two distinct tasks: generating facial images and calculating optical flow. We also show that the generated domain-specific inputs can be leveraged by other students, trained via self-supervision, to perform additional tasks. We highlight the potential for our method to support a broader range of problems and more complex expert functions compared to existing approaches. We also discuss some possible adaptations of our proposed method to address additional challenges. We analyze a stochastic Newton method for solving the distributed average consensus congestion game and a similarly structured stochastic blockwise Newton algorithm for general distributed convex optimization. In these contexts, individual nodes receive private, gradient-correlated data streams that must be combined efficiently. The proposed methods utilize in-stream, locally-calculated Newton updates,enabling the elimination of gradient estimates and alleviating a major challenge in stochastic Newton methods. The methods are proven to converge at a linear rate under suitable Platt conditions and are shown to outperform stochastic gradient methods, particularly in scenarios with strongly convex objectives, where convergence rates are tied to the Newton quadratic convergence rate. Notably, this performance improves over existing distributed Newton methods while matching state-of-the-art convergence rates. The methods are supported by comprehensive simulation studies. The principal contribution lies in a novel stochastic Newton component, encompassing novel convergence rate analyses for the distributed algorithms. Previous studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of machine learning algorithms in detecting hate-speech in English, but there is a significant gap in research on languages spoken primarily in India. Considering that half of the country's population speaks languages such as Hindi and Bengali that have yet to be extensively explored in hate-speech research, we conducted a study utilizing a novel dataset containing hate-speech examples in these languages. Our research team labeled an extensive collection of social media posts, creating a comprehensive dataset for hate-speech detection in Hindi and Bengali. By comparing the performance of various neural networks, we identified that a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model delivered the highest accuracy in hate-speech detection in both languages, achieving 91.7% accuracy in Hindi and 88.8% accuracy in Bengali. Moreover, we explored the applicability of transfer learning to Hindi and Bengali, and our results indicate that it is possible to develop Hindi and Bengali hate-speech detection models by leveraging a transferred model from English, yielding 85.6% and 81.5% accuracies, respectively. Ultimately, we proposed a potential research direction that could bridge the language detection gap by developing a universal model for hate-speech across various languages. Such a model could be trained through a multi-step approach, starting with English before moving to low-resource languages like Hindi and Bengali, which in turn can inform the detection of similar languages. Our study also provides critical insights that could guide future research as hate-speech detection becomes an increasingly pressing concern across languages. The labeled dataset created in this study is publicly available on our GitHub repository at: https://github.com/protapmehedi/Hate-Speech-Dataset. In nuclear and particle physics experiments utilizing Gas Time Projection Chambers (GTPCs) for recoil detection, the ability to precisely track multiple tracks is crucial. This requirement is particularly challenging on a coarse readout grid in existing setups. We introduce a new analysis that's able to accurately identify the direction and location of tracks, as well as detect the presence of recoils, through the use of the scalar dipole and angular momentum operators applied to projected charge distributions. Our study demonstrates the resilience of these operators under various signal-to-noise ratios and reconstruction resolutions. We found that using the scalar dipole operator yields optimal results, outperforming existing GTPC approaches by over 30% and enabling the detection of recoils with a spatial resolution of at least 0.5 mm, even with poor signal conditions. Additionally, the proposed method can be seamlessly integrated into existing analysis pipelines with minimal modifications, making it highly adaptable across a wide range of experiments. We primarily focus our analysis on GTPC-based Neutrinoless Double Beta Decay investigations but emphasize the broad applicability of this approach across various gaseous detectors used in nuclear and particle physics experiments. Our study's findings are accompanied by a public repository containing the necessary code for replicating the results, as well as sample data derived from simulations. This resource can be accessed at https://github.com/mkchouza/GTPC-operators. We plan to further improve these operators' performance as described in our related study (arXiv:2202.02264). When incorporating machine learning into high-stakes decision-making processes, there's an acknowledged risk of biased outputs. Although numerous studies have explored the biases present in these calculations, there is less research examining the impact of these biases when experts utilize the machine-generated information to form their opinions. This research centers on the connection between automatic hazard assessment in commercial driving and driving license renewal, a decision-making process within the United States Department of Transportation. We discover that drivers, especially those who are more skilled and experienced, tend to have lower hazard ratings assigned by machines, yet these ratings do not reflect the experts' opinions in all instances. When factoring in the context of an individual's past performance as a driver, the experts' views diverge from the machine outputs. This study highlights the difficulties in synchronizing human and machine intelligence, particularly when accounting for the intricacies of commercial driving. It also emphasizes that merely reducing machine biases in isolated instances may not be sufficient in obtaining fair outcomes in complex systems. To address these complexities, experts provided more nuanced evaluations than the machine outputs, underscoring the value of expert input in deciding the validity of machine-generated information. This study provides a foundation for examining the interplay between human and machine intelligence in high-stakes decision-making processes and proposes a low-cost method to enhance the fairness of these decisions. Ultimately, our research points to a promising strategy for developing more fair and equitable models by combining machine learning with periodic 'turbocharging' from experts to address intricate contextual aspects. These findings can be applied in a broader array of domains, as well. The objective of the Out-of-Category challenge is to assess a model's ability to generalize to categories not seen during training. The specific requirement is for a model to successfully classify images from an unseen category when trained on another unrelated image dataset. We conducted the challenge using a dataset comprised of images from various animal categories and compared the performance of different image classification techniques. The challenge key finding highlights that even high-accuracy image classifiers struggle to generalize to unrelated categories, particularly when there's limited data available. Moreover, fine-tuning pre-trained models using small datasets results in poor generalization to unrelated categories. Notably, cross-entropy loss proved ineffective in achieving accurate generalization to unseen categories. It appears that better results can be achieved by training models specifically for each target category using their respective datasets. The challenge findings suggest that better loss functions and architectures are required to successfully generalize to unrelated image classification tasks. The challenge is contingent on future outcomes; if successful, the challenge winner will receive $10,000. The current work serves as a preliminary exploration for the Out-of-Category challenge. Further investigations are necessary to confirm the challenge's outcomes and find improved solutions to the Out-of-Category problem. The Out-of-Category challenge is unique among data out-of-distribution generalization challenges in that it involves distinct image categories, unrelated to the training dataset. It shares some similarities with distribution shift challenges like Domain-Adversarial Neural Network (DANN) and with the Dog vs. Cat challenge, which also focuses on out-of-category classification. The Out-of-Category challenge is the first to assess a model's ability to classify images from categories not seen during training using image classification techniques. The challenge is distinct from other image classification challenges in that it involves small datasets. The transport properties of graphene, particularly in the context of spin-dependent conductivity, make it an ideal platform for exploring spin-related electronic phenomena. Recent findings have confirmed that graphene hosts a non-zero global spin polarization under certain charge injections. Nevertheless, establishing reliable devices to facilitate spin current control is an ongoing challenge. To address this issue, our research focuses on designing edge-functionalized graphene devices in the form of nanoribbons, which are configured as parallel Rashba-Edelstein devices. These devices are capable of modulating a spin-polarized charge current with an adjustable spin orientation, as well as controlling the injection of spin-polarized current through graphene-based spin valves. The underlying mechanism involves a distinctive transport phenomenon in which the spin Hall effect amplifies the overall spin orientation. Importantly, our results show that this amplified spin effect can be observed at room temperature, which holds significant potential for integrating these devices into spintronics based on room temperature. Moreover, our device designs enable the development of devices that can convert a charge current into a light beam while exhibiting substantial magnification of the spin orientation. These device concepts may contribute to a range of innovative spintronic applications, including spin-induced photonic devices. This research focuses on establishing Korovkin-type theorem variants in the context of weakly nonlinear, monotone operators applied to multi-variable Banach lattices. Specifically, we consider $\mathcal{A}$ as a collection of such operators mapping $\mathbb{R}^d$ to a Banach space defined as $\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^s$. We also introduce the notion of weakly nonlinear operators satisfying the condition that the first-order Taylor expansion of $\mathcal{B}[x]_j$ about $x_j=0$ is equal to $b_j[\cdot]$ for each $j \in \{1, 2, \ldots, d\}$, where $\mathcal{B}[x] = (b_1[\cdot], \ldots, b_d[\cdot]) \in \mathcal{A}$. The primary results in this paper describe the consistency theorems for sequences of functions that are continuous and bounded for these types of operators applied to Banach spaces or operator spaces. Moreover, we extend Kolmogorov's entropy-like definitions to the multi-variable setting with functions of $E \times \Omega$ to compact domains of $\mathbb{R}^s$, where $E, \Omega \in \mathbb{R}^d$, and provide the necessary entropy-type estimates. The research also explores the extension of P.-M. Sarachicole's findings to the setting of operator spaces. The proof of the main results in this paper relies on the linearization property of weakly nonlinear operators and the application of Schauder's basis constructions, such as de la Vallée Poussin and Szász, to compact domains of $\mathbb{R}^d$. The results in this paper can be considered the Korovkin theorem variants of choice in the contemporary functional analysis setting. The research presented in this paper extends the findings to the setting of operator spaces. This work introduces a novel mathematical approach grounded in the unscaled Schrödinger equation, employing an intricate combination of three types of complex scaling transformations. We leverage this method to examine the behavior of certain complex scaling singularities in the presence of extremely strong direct current electric fields. We utilize this technique to predict the emergence points, widths, and resonant frequencies of dressed resonances arising from the discontinuity of the atomic polarizability at zero DC strength. We apply this method to the hydrogen atom and the H$^{-}$ ion to investigate their respective resonances. We further demonstrate that this method can be adapted to tackle multi-lectron problems by utilizing it to find the eigenvalues of a model one-electron system interacting with a fixed proton via a distance-dependent potential featuring a 'hard-wall'. We show that this method can produce solutions describing resonance states that arise due to coupling with the continuum. We derive an explicit expression for the scaling factor 't', eliminating the parameter 'w' in the problem, and we discover that the eigenvalue problem we've formulated becomes identical to a well-known problem in physics, involving a typical 'inverted harmonic oscillator'. We successfully calculate the eigenvalues of this model, apply a perturbation calculation to find the shifts in resonant frequencies caused by DC field strength, and compare these results with the outcomes of a different method used in prior studies. We note that although our method is more complicated than the one it's supposed to replicate, it's actually less complicated than the one it's supposed to improve upon! We highlight that although our method relies on the complex scaling transformation, which can potentially lead to the szymanski phenomenon, our specific approach doesn't employ any of three time-delay definitions associated with the problem. We further observe that although the problem we've formulated is independent of the complex parameter 't', it's actually easier to solve when the parameter 't' is chosen wisely. We argue that choosing the parameter wisely can potentially address the zymanstki phenomenon in the problem, making the method even simpler! We propose that the correct value of the parameter 't' can be obtained through a new approach to the problem, where it's based on the behavior of the wave function near a specific point in the problem, rather than a certain mathematical property associated with the problem. The Sinkhorn algorithm, a numerical method for solving the Schrödinger problem, relies on solving three equations recursively. Although it has been proven convergent under specific conditions, research has revealed that, under certain circumstances, this algorithm may converge to an inconsistent solution, leading to a scenario where no such solution exists. Our aim is to thoroughly investigate these instances. By examining the problem in both a one-dimensional and multi-dimensional context, we demonstrate that, even though the algorithm appears to converge, it may still fail to produce a solution for specific metric or transport configurations. However, our simulations also show that, as the scaling factor approaches infinity, the Sinkhorn algorithm tends to converge toward a solution for particular types of metrics. This behavior is attributed to the appearance of an inconsistent convex combination of the data constraints. Furthermore, we explore an improved version of the algorithm, incorporating a regularization term, which can be either fixed or decaying, and demonstrate its efficacy in producing a solution for a multi-dimensional example where the standard Sinkhorn algorithm converges to an inconsistent solution. Our research demonstrates that, despite its popularity, the Sinkhorn algorithm is not always reliable in all cases. However, by modifying the algorithm with a regularization term, even in a small amount, we can achieve a solution for a wide range of data. These improved algorithms, with regularization, have the potential to expand the applicability of the Sinkhorn algorithm. As such, we can use them to produce high-quality transport maps even in cases that the unregularized algorithm converges to an inconsistent solution. Moreover, we speculate that, with the rise of machine learning, problems with inconsistent solutions may become more prevalent, leading to an evaluation of the theoretical framework and improvements to the Sinkhorn algorithm. Our findings are based on analyses of 5,086,851,190 hours of surveillance data from
Boston areas with functioning cameras. We explored the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic
on movement patterns in the city's sub-districts, assessing how they changed over
time and which demographic groups were most affected. We discovered that the
population's spatial mixing improved significantly during the pandemic, yet this
gain was subsequently undermined by the varied responses to pandemic-related
restrictions. We particularly noticed a significant decrease in public space
interactions among low-income residents, whereas high-income residents tended to
maintain their social connections. By combining observational data with income-
based segmentation, we showed that the pandemic exacerbated income-based
segregation in urban areas. Our research emphasizes the importance of diverse
population mixing, as well as the need for more effective pandemic policies that do
not disproportionately benefit affluent residents. Lastly, we believe that the
long-term consequences of the pandemic's impact on urban planning should be
investigated. 

Our study's data covers a period from August 2019 to October 2021, focusing on
three phases: pre-pandemic August-February, pandemic-related
restrictions-February-June, and post-pandemic June-October. We used demographic
projection and mapping techniques to determine the demographic structure of each
area and assess how their income diversity changed. 

Notably, our study reveals that the pandemic's effects on movement patterns
differed significantly depending on the area's income diversity. While residents in
well-mixed areas showed more resilience, areas with less income diversity were more
affected by the pandemic, with a more pronounced decline in movement patterns.
However, under better-mixed conditions, public space interactions among low-income
residents surpassed those of high-income residents, contradicting existing research.
Moreover, areas with less income diversity experienced greater variability in
movement patterns, and their recovery was slower, while those with higher income
diversity displayed more consistent and stable patterns. 

In particular, our study observes that the pandemic exacerbated the historical
trend of income-based segregation in Boston and other similar cities. 

Our analysis is unique in several ways:

1) It automatically identifies and evaluates the effect of pandemic-related
restrictions on movement patterns in each area.

2) It assesses the impact of policies on different demographic groups using
demographic projection techniques.

3) It provides a quantitative and robust test of the relationship between

The search for Extended Radio Synchrotron Emission (ERSE) in galaxies can aid the detection of dark matter, as its intensity correlates with dark matter halos. A previous survey found ERSE in approximately 12% of a sample of 60 galaxies via the SRT at 12 GHz, but a smaller sample size precluded drawing firm conclusions. To gather more data, a new sample of 40 spiral and irregular galaxies was selected and observed at 33 GHz. Although the SRT observations discovered ERSE in approximately 25% of these galaxies, the authors couldn't establish this frequency distribution as significantly different from 12 GHz. Combining the results from the two samples, the authors found a total of 32 galaxies with ERSE out of 100, suggesting that ERSE exists in around 32% $\pm$ 8% of galaxies. A subsequent high-frequency observation at 8.6 GHz was carried out on four galaxies, revealing that ERSE in galaxies also exhibits frequency-dependent emission. Moreover, in such galaxies both intensity and spectral index were observed to vary with frequency. A detailed analysis of the spectral indices suggested that ERSE could originate from multiple components with different origins. Specifically, a low-frequency component with a spectral index around -0.8 could be produced by primordial magnetic fields, while a high-frequency component with a spectral index around -3 might instead originate from the interaction of relativistic particles with the interstellar medium or structure. A tool for checking for these emissions in nearby galaxies has been created and hosted at [www.francescosacco.com](http://www.francescosacco.com).

The Fréchet distance, a widely recognized metric for measuring curvature-based shape similarity, particularly in child care activity recognition, remains challenging to approximate. Despite this, some studies propose approximate distance metrics, like $\epsilon$-truncation and Lombardi's simplified path, which introduce a specific error $\epsilon$ and provide bounds for close-neighbor search, but these have yet to demonstrate tight bounds, leading other studies to employ probabilistic methods, which, although achieving tighter error bounds, decrease query processing efficiency, a crucial factor in many applications. This study presents a new, efficient, and high-correctness algorithm for close-neighbor search based on a modified 1-center approach, which omits segments causing the largest distance increases while preserving crucial sections, along with two alternative methods that offer higher processing efficiency. The study conducts a comprehensive analysis of the new algorithms, proving they offer tight bounds, efficient processing, and high quality results, which are further confirmed through experiments performed on child care time series. The study establishes the existence of a constant $C$ such that the time required to answer each query is proportional to $n^{1+\frac{\epsilon}{C}}$ and $n^{2-\frac{\epsilon}{C}}$ for the first and second algorithms, respectively, which remain insensitive to the parameter $\epsilon$ for small values. These results, confirmed in experiments over various child care time series, display high resistance to changes for both algorithms. In this work, we explore the task of Contextual Named Entity Retrieval (CNER) as a part of Answer Selection, aiming to connect a context with its relevant named entity descriptions. CNER involves finding the most appropriate entity description given a context, but current methods focus solely on matching words between the context and target descriptions, without considering the overall relevance of the descriptions. Consequently, they struggle with selections that are contextually valid but lack relevance. We introduce a new approach that addresses this by comparing both context and description contexts with the desired term relevance, using a neural network that learns description-specific context embeddings. This enables the network to select descriptions that not only align contextually but also are more relevant and resilient to variations in descriptions. Experimental results on both general and dedicated CNER benchmarks demonstrate significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art CNER methods, underscoring the effectiveness of our term relevance response strategy. We have made our source code and trained models publicly available. Further analysis through shuffling experiments on both Answer Selection and Term Extraction tasks reveals that our term relevance response strategy remains superior even after accounting for methodical biases. Moreover, we have identified that our method is particularly beneficial in domains where descriptions lack sufficient context information. We conduct this investigation on a new high-variability CNER benchmark recently proposed as CNER-HV. We have found that our term relevance response strategy enhances CNER-HV ranking performance across all listed domains. We recommend that our method be used in conjunction with existing CNER models to provide a more comprehensive ranking. Our study is the first to address the importance of term relevance in CNER and contributes new datasets, evaluation processes, and domain insights that could be valuable for the natural language community. The study highlights the value of term relevance response in CNER and Answer Selection contexts. Finally, we have identified that our method is complementary and can enhance the performance of existing CNER models, thus providing improved results in both CNER and Answer Selection tasks. The study is an extension of our UCL CNER competition contributions, where we have now further developed the idea of term relevance response. Interactive visualizations are particularly effective at analyzing complex data but users often struggle with decision-making tasks involving multiple related values over extended periods. While visualizations can be improved by displaying trends and seasonality, internal fluctuations, and individual data points, it's unclear how users prefer to see these components in longitudinal data. We conducted surveys with 400 researchers and non-researchers, and interviewed 16 professionals, to identify the preferences of users analyzing longitudinal data. Our findings reveal that users prefer visualizations offering flexible panning, trend visualization, and easy access to detailed data points, especially when multiple related data points need to be compared. We discovered three primary user goals when working with longitudinal data: in-depth analysis, education, and presentation. We designed novel visualizations addressing these goals, and incorporating users' preferred features, and conducted another study to validate our design choices. The resulting base-classified structure-longitudinal (BSL) visualization allows users to seamlessly switch between displaying data trends over extended periods and in-depth comparisons of individual data points at any point during the analysis. By integrating users' preferences and decision-making tasks into the design, the BSL visualization enhances users' productivity when analyzing longitudinal data. It facilitates data exploration through long-term trends and in-depth comparisons, and users can customize the visualization to suit their analysis methods and data types without compromising their analysis. We believe the BSL visualization can empower users to work more efficiently with various types of complex data. It can be applied to multivariate time series, longitudinal data, and data visualizations with additional attributes like temperature, which was confirmed in our expert review. Clinical research and care decision-making both rely heavily on understanding how similar patient health outcomes are to those of others in the past. However, standard methods we use today to compare patients don't take into account the complex interplay of systems and signals within the human body, nor the varied and limited information available from electronic health records (EHRs), which are noisy and contain gaps in patient data. To address these challenges and variations, we're proposing a new approach - heterogeneous resemblance - to develop personalized comparisons for EHRs, which focuses on finding patients with similar sequences of events and similar predictions of future outcomes. We're testing this approach through the creation of a novel graph neural network, which we demonstrate on three different tasks within the field of EHRs and show that it outperforms existing comparison methods. Furthermore, we're using our approach to study the similarities and differences between patients who have COVID-19 and those who do not, which highlights the ability of our method to explore these topics. We believe that by accounting for the diversity of human systems and sources, EHR-based heterogeneous resemblance will lead to more accurate and more equitable patient comparisons. We're making our code available so that others can build upon our work. Using a novel approach, we successfully initial alignment of lidar data across various datasets in the lyft lidar kit and MoCap benchmark datasets. We compare the performance of traditional Pseudo-Measure filter with this neural network filter to understand their effectiveness in peak peak registration accuracy. Through experiments, we demonstrate that the DNN Filter can reduce systematic bias up to 80% more effectively than the PMF and also provide better accuracy in final pose estimation in distribution-to-distribution scan matching. Additionally, our results reveal that the DNN Filter can be combined with the PMF to achieve even higher levels of accuracy, which highlights its potential as a useful method for validating and refining odometry data. We also explore the key factors that could further enhance the performance of the DNN Filter and outline potential areas for future development. Ultimately, this study emerges as a viable solution for correcting systematic systematic errors in lidar data. Our research focuses on the implications of modulated primordial features, particularly those with a periodic nature, on cosmic microwave background observations through high-energy particle collisions. These primordial features could stem from variables like massive fields affecting cosmological inflation or specific models of inflationary dynamics. Given that recent CMB data fails to support standard cosmological models with high confidence, the possibility of modulated primordial features as described in literature cannot be ruled out. Our analysis indicates that the distinctive signatures of feature-motivated models with oscillating fields are detectable only when the number of oscillations is substantial, beyond a hundred, and the frequency of oscillations exceeds the range of energies encompassing CMB data, typically between 10 and 100. Moreover, if the primordial features are driven by a variable with quantum fluctuations smaller than the differences between successive features, the resulting features exhibit correlations that reduce their visibility. To make our discussion more concrete, we outline a theory called Variability-Motivated Inflation, incorporating derivatives of a Galileon shift field, and demonstrate that the influence of these derivatives on inflationary dynamics introduces both modulations and correlations in the power spectrum. Our calculations show that the number of oscillations, the frequency, and amplitude of the features depend on the properties of the non-minimal sector, the number of quanta along the shift field, and the properties of the scalar responsible for temperature variations. Our research highlights the capacity of high-energy particle collisions to reveal evidence of modulated primordial features, even when the number of oscillations, frequency, and amplitude are small, regardless of the complexity of the underlying inflationary model. Moreover, in the event that the measurements of $n_s$ and $\log A_s$ do not deviate from the best-fit values, the observable effects of feature-motivated models with low-frequency oscillations can be determined solely by the fundamental parameters controlling the primordial features and the properties of the quantum fluctuations during cosmic inflation. In particular, for variation-motivated inflationary models with low-frequency oscillations, for example those driven by a variable with quantum fluctuations smaller than the differences between successive features, cross-checks between constraints on primordial features and constraints on Higgs boson masses could help establish the characteristics of the fundamental sector responsible for cosmic inflation. Our research presents an alternative interpretation of the observed deviation from the best-fit values of the spectral index reported in the 2018 Planck dataset, one that does not involve non-Gaussianity. It's challenging for users who are not experts in deep learning to identify the specific parts of an image that influence a classification decision. Recent studies attempting to explain deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) focus on discovering key areas within images, but they typically fail to reveal why these areas are crucial. In contrast, we propose introducing filter focus - a latent factor affecting image classification that is imprinted on data by a particular CNN - into each image location. By assuming that each location within an image shares a common factor, we utilize semantic regions as pseudo-labels and an EM algorithm to estimate the latent factor. The latent factor consists of unique visual patterns at each location and a common factor across locations. The key regions are then identified as those with the highest common factor values. In our evaluation, we found that this latent factor, referred to as filter focus, effectively explains the classification decisions of CNNs on various tasks, including fine-grained products classification and coarse-grained scene classification. Moreover, we conducted an usability study with non-experts, who provided verbal explanations for the areas with high filter focus values; these explanations significantly outperformed the baselines. You can find more information at our website: \url{https://filterfocus.net}. Additionally, we offer a user-friendly tool called the Visual Interpreter, which allows users to interactively understand CNN-based classification models. You can access this tool at \url{https://visual-interpreter.net}. As an example of the usability of our method, in Figure 1, we show how it helps reveal the reasons behind the classification of a Converse Chuck Taylor All Star as "a pair of sandals". The top two visual patterns at the right have a strong connection to the classification result. Interestingly, we discovered that the CNN produced the correct classification despite being trained with very few images of sandals from the data set it was trained on - only two images. Such accuracy with limited data is characteristic of CNNs that were trained on very competitive data sets. Our method is not limited to explaining the classification of sandals, but rather it effectively explains the classification of any product, including "handbags", "vehicles", "dogs", and "airplanes", as well as coarse-grained scenes such as "beaches", "deserts", "forest", and "mountains". To assess the authenticity of digital evidence, particularly in forensic face-to-face investigations, it's essential to determine if a face has been digitally manipulated. Since existing methods primarily focus on detecting deliberate alterations, a new approach is developed to reveal subtle, reversible changes within compressed video and images. A novel framework combining reversible image transformation and the Bayesian Neural Network is proposed, allowing for the creation of training data with original and manipulated images that are identical in format. By employing this transformed data in the training of an autoencoder, and subsequently applying it to identify original faces, an accurate rate is achieved without prior knowledge of the original images. The proposed technique is demonstrated with popular image codecs including JPEG, MPEG, H.264, and PNG, as well as compared with existing methods using face manipulation benchmarks. When applied to such equations, the method always requires a minimum of one evaluation per step, except in rare cases of vanishing derivatives. Moreover, the method's local convergence properties remain unchanged but, due to its variable step nature, may lead to larger errors in some instances. Interestingly, the method's behavior is comparable to that of the optimally smoothed QSS method in many scenarios. To address potential superconvergence issues, we introduced a simple smoothing post-processing step, which significantly improves the method's performance without affecting local convergence. This suggests that further adjustments are necessary to guarantee satisfactory results in all scenarios. The origin of the hot intergalactic medium (IGM) within dwarf galaxies is an
actively debated issue. This article focuses on the characteristics of the IGM
within dwarf galaxy halos, specifically exploring its temperature,
baryon fraction, and the relationships between the IGM, the galaxies, and dark matter.
We examine various cooling theories as potential explanations for the IGM and
propose that, at a dwarf galaxy mass level, the IGM is primarily composed of heated
galactic outflows which can penetrate deep into galaxy halos. We also discuss
how galactic outflows may be influenced by reacceration from supergalactic scales
and other potential factors, such as heat via turbulent friction and radiative
heating from the cosmic background. We suggest that galactic outflows, with
input from feedback processes, serve as the primary driving force behind the
enrichment of the IGM within dwarf galaxies through outflow penetration.
Consequently, the enriched IGM can then be incorporated into new stellar
formations or halo accretion events, thus perpetuating cycles of matter
interchange within galaxy halos, albeit a more subtle version of such processes
compared to what is observed in larger galaxies. Furthermore, the characteristics
of dwarf galaxy IGMs hold significant implications for our understanding of the
cosmic evolution of dwarf galaxies as sites of metal production. Specifically,
the production of heavy elements within dwarf galaxy bulges or halos can be
significantly influenced by prior enrichment of the IGM within these galaxy
components and could explain observed variations in cosmic metallicity at
intermediate redshifts if these variations stem from differences in galaxy mass,
with more massive galaxies producing more metal-enriched IGMs. If, however,
enrichment from galactic outflows within low-mass dwarf galaxies is not a primary
factor, then it suggests an underestimation of the role of feedback in driving
enrichment, or else the IGM within dwarf galaxies serves as an anomalous IGM
configuration. Ultimately, the characteristics of the IGM within dwarf galaxies
serve as an important benchmark for supermassive galaxy black holes at the lower
mass end of their predicted range; specifically, the prevention of continuous
feedback cycles from galaxy-wide outflow penetration may explain the apparent
break in the relationship between BH mass and host galaxy mass at the lower mass

Text-clip retrieval is an essential technology for zero-shot text-to-text applications such as text-based image description and vice versa. Current approaches rely on a pre-trained transformer that encodes images and generates text embeddings. However, they suffer from slow browsing and poor accuracy due to their fixed structure. To address these limitations, we introduce TS2-Net, a novel retrieval model, which achieves both efficiency and accuracy by incorporating a token shift and selection mechanism. TS2-Net's dynamic token selection process enables both browse speed and accuracy to be customized. Our token shift model browses input tokens with a fixed position shift, while the sample size can be adjusted to balance performance and computation cost. Our TS2-Net approach outperforms the existing state-of-the-art by a large margin, demonstrating superiority over a comprehensive set of robust metrics and zero-shot settings. In the case of AdS space, our computation involves the holographic stress tensor using a variational method and we compare these to stress tensors derived from the dual CFT using a radial Hamiltonian and via the Schrödinger representation. There is an established method for transforming a variogram into a covariance function and vice versa. This usually involves making simplifying assumptions about the underlying geometry to convert spatial measurements into a regression model, often employing a squared exponential kernel in the process. This paper presents a tool to generate kernels on surfaces, which are represented by analytical functions with parameters that need to be specified. These parameters can be optimized using the coefficients obtained from fitting the corresponding covariance functions. The proposed approach allows for efficient modeling of surfaces through a combination of linear and non-linear components and anisotropy. The surface of a 2D noise layer is used as an example to demonstrate the effectiveness of this method. Additionally, this technique can be used to identify which factors most influence a complex phenomenon, as well as recover relevant information when conducting post-hoc analysis after collecting new data to supplement existing datasets.

Future high-energy muon colliders face a challenge due to beam-induced disruption in their detectors. This problem will clearly affect their performance, necessitating careful reduction of associated noise. In this study, researchers examine potential methods for reducing beam-induced noise in these devices. These techniques include using liquid helium, moving detector components, using advanced materials, enhancing vacuum conditions, improving design with the beam in mind, and using thin film detectors. A dedicated simulation tool was developed to evaluate these strategies' effectiveness. Initial findings reveal that several methods can effectively mitigate beam-induced noise, with particular emphasis on using liquid helium and advanced design with the beam in mind. These methods show promising results in reducing noise by several orders of magnitude. This reduction successfully prevents performance degradation from this source, paving the way for optimized detector designs that can take full advantage of their potential. Additionally, researchers explored thin film detectors' capabilities as low-noise, high-range detectors in tin-tungsten X-ray imaging at the LHe temperature. While they require further development, these innovative detectors may offer unique benefits. Ultimately, a multi-faceted approach centered on understanding and influencing beam-detector interactions is likely to yield the most effective reduction in beam-induced noise. This work serves as a foundational resource for muon collider detectors, providing essential considerations for optimizing these devices to overcome beam-induced challenges. These considerations are sure to be applicable to a broader range of future devices as well. Moreover, researchers suggest that future research investigate advanced materials and nanotechnology solutions to further reduce beam-induced noise and benefit future colliders. This study is expected to serve as a crucial reference for future research in detector design for muon colliders. Moreover, researchers recommend that future research in beam-induced noise be broadened to include other innovative materials and technological solutions for optimizing detector performance. Software developers widely acknowledge the importance of unit testing as a crucial aspect of their work cycle, allowing for swift detection and resolution of coding errors. However, test code can be compromised by suboptimal design or implementation practices that may diminish the effectiveness of unit tests. These suboptimal design practices are referred to as 'test smells.' Although theoretical frameworks propose various solutions to address test smells, empirical evidence regarding their impact on quality is still scarce. In this study, we aim to gather developers' views on three prominent test smells: 1) redundant code, 2) code that is not used, and 3) complex assertions. We surveyed 1,597 software developers via a Google form and obtained 226 useable responses. Our results indicate that while developers are aware of the first test smell's negative consequences, its prevalence is not a significant concern. In contrast, unused code is considered a relatively minor issue with fewer negative consequences. Interestingly, high-level assertions with negative consequences are not a primary concern for developers, likely because they are not frequently encountered. These findings align with existing best practices for avoiding these test smells. We discuss the implications of our results and suggest strategies for further research. Furthermore, we investigate the connection between test smells and their impact on the maintainability of test code, providing insights into the maturation of testing practices. Interestingly, our results suggest an inverse relationship between the difficulty of removing test smells and developers' willingness to implement refactoring changes. We observe an initial willingness to address test smells for the first time, which gradually decreases over time. Our results demonstrate that test smells can serve as indicators of growing or declining testing practices. The context in which developers work may also influence their attitudes towards test smells; those who encounter test smells as part of legacy code tend to view them as normal practice. In contrast, those who do not work with legacy code generally consider these smells as areas for improvement. Ultimately, the awareness and willingness of developers to address test smells are key factors in refining testing practices. We believe that enhancing awareness through empirical research can foster a more positive outlook on test smells among software developers. Our results encourage further studies that focus on the process of detecting and removing test smells, particularly by exploring alternative detection methods and refining best practices for remediation. Additionally, our results demonstrate that the success of empirical software engineering efforts often rely on the diversity of participants, which may vary based on factors such as geographical location, work environment, or personal preferences, which can, in turn, affect their various preferences and priorities. In various social networks, reference materials, network planning, urban design, and drug effects, graph representation plays a pivotal role. It's essential to adapt graphs as they change over time; this requirement leads to the study of evolving graphs. Unlike static graphs, where direct applications are common, evolving graphs benefit from time-aware embeddings that account for structure, network changes, and circuit analysis at different points. This review explores the methods and models behind evolving graph embeddings, discussing both historical and current approaches, and identifying challenges and potential areas for future research, including the application of emerging technologies like graph neural networks. Additionally, it provides an overview of the first-ever dedicated evolving graph embedding workshop, highlighting prominent topics and discussions. With growing interest in evolving graph embeddings, we hope this survey inspires more researchers to tackle related challenges............ 

Evolving graphs have gained significant attention over the years, leading to the development of various embedding methods that consider different aspects, network changes, and temporal information. This research reviews the primary types of evolving graphs (temporal, growth, and multi-faceted), associated embeddings (vertex, edge, path, and general), and discusses emerging challenges and potential areas for future growth. 

Temporally evolving graphs draw structure from multiple snapshots of a single graph, and embeddings can be static (ignoring changes) or dynamic (reflecting evolving relationships). Growth evolving graphs expand through the addition of new nodes over time, and embeddings can be understood from different perspectives - static, focusing on core concepts, and dynamic, focusing on relationships. Multi-faceted evolving graphs are characterized by changes in nodes, edges, orientation, and other aspects, and their embeddings can be studied from different viewpoints - static, focusing on core concepts versus dynamic, focusing on relationships.

In terms of analysis, some methods evaluate the impact of network changes, others, the structural properties of nodes, and yet others propose representations that incorporate temporal information. This dichotomy of approaches is taken a step further by discussing general evolving graph embeddings, which can be studied from core or relational perspectives, leading to a discussion of applications, which is particularly significant in the context of graph embeddings. 

Graph embeddings have numerous applications in geometry, data recovery, image processing, computer vision, natural language understanding, and other fields. This review explores the methods and models behind evolving graph embeddings, discussing historical and current approaches, and identifying challenges and potential areas for future growth, and it provides an overview of the first-ever dedicated evolving graph embedding workshop, highlighting prominent topics

Recently, a research team reported highly accurate ground state calculations for the $^7$H nucleus, consisting of a 2-proton and 5-neutron system. To further demonstrate the utility of these calculations, we suggest treating the $^7$H ground state as a $^3$H (with one proton and two neutrons) and four neutrons, combined. To validate this approach, we first generate a $^3$H ground state solution using the Monte Carlo diffusion method and then combine it with a four-neutron correlated ground state obtained through the Monte Carlo shell model with the SkP interaction. Our approach allows us to determine the ground and excited states of the $^{4}$Ne nucleus as a $^3$H and one neutron configuration. By employing this method, we can investigate the spectral distribution of $^7$H, confirming that its energy spectrum is dominated by a $^3$H and four neutrons configuration. Ultimately, the research highlights the potential benefits of collaborating between public health officials and private data sources as complementary tools to aid in the management of public health crises. By leveraging deep learning models, the camera's orientation and pose can be rapidly determined, even in scenarios with minimal or no visual tracking. Furthermore, the camera's parameters can be instantly applied to the robotic arm's end effector, enabling the tool to be reoriented accordingly. Our method was tested using the ITSD dataset, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing approaches. Additionally, a control plane was established in our study to ensure that the camera and robotic arm maintain synchronized orientations. Our experiments showcase that this approach successfully generalizes across various domains, particularly when there are distinct labelling standards for camera and robotic arm positions. Lastly, the method was successfully evaluated on the T-6D dataset to calculate the 6D camera pose. We introduce a range of action generation models, including one that utilizes beta-distributed mixing weights, and we create action sets by drawing from these models. We then establish tight upper and lower bounds on the rate of almost exact confidence intervals for the estimated parameter vector's projection onto the span of observed actions. Depending on the action generation model, we either fix the rate or demonstrate that the rate can be improved by using any number of (potentially many) additional actions. Additionally, we show that modifying the standard linear bandit approach by projecting the parameter vector onto the span of observed actions yields the optimal regret rate for beta-distributed action generation models, but not for others. Finally, we explore the implications of our findings on commonly used inference techniques for linear bandits and provide numerical examples to support our results. They show that the rate of usual confidence intervals for linear bandit estimates is suboptimal, except when the action set consists of a diverse, uniformly distributed selection of actions. We also demonstrate that even a long sequence of (nearly) exactly confident intervals does not guarantee the optimal rate, except when the action set is nearly diverse. Our analysis reveals that the key factor precluding optimal performance is the inferential independence between actions, which can be achieved with independent, uniformly distributed over a large enough set of row spaces. Based on these insights, we propose an easily implementable, diversity-promoting confidence interval for linear bandit estimates that closely matches the upper bound we established. Despite the introduction of a gap, the distinct characteristics of its valleys still give rise to an unusual phenomenon called the valley Hall effect, which allows electrons to move in an circular pattern through a 2D material by generating counter-propagating electrons on either side of a gap. Our research implies that the orbital Hall effect may be experienced in two-gapped graphene, providing a new avenue for the study of this unique phenomenon.  Our experiments also open up fresh possibilities for the discovery of the orbital Hall effect in newly developed materials with two gaps, such as HgTe quantum wells with an inverted band structure.  The orbital Hall effect may potentially be observed in a variety of materials with two gaps, providing an exciting prospect for the discovery of this unusual phenomenon. We introduce an innovative training strategy for sign language recognition that leverages sign language and speech alignments through attention-based convolutional sequence alignment and relies on minimal speech-based training data.
Our approach removes the inter-domain difference by matching speech and sign language into a common domain using CycleGAN, and incorporates inter-domain loss to minimize remaining discrepancies.
Through experiments on the Bench test dataset, over-labeled through eye-tracking, we demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms baseline models that use inter-domain loss alone, improving Word Error Rate by over 25%, and matches or surpasses the performance of fully supervised models. Additional analysis reveals that the majority of errors made by our system involve small positional mistakes in handling overlapping hand and mouth movements. This has important implications for future research as our technique appears to be more sensitive to hand mouth overlaps than fully supervised models. To tackle this challenge, we incorporate Deep Active Learning, a highly adaptive framework that effectively reduces data uncertainty. This involves combining a predictive model of robot behavior with an uncertainty quantification model for images, allowing for online selection of optimal visual inputs. By iteratively analyzing the images with the highest uncertainty and corresponding low predicted outcomes, the robot learns to anticipate and achieve its desired state. This approach is demonstrated in a practical application where the NAO robot visualizes and visits a target location, and it exemplifies the benefits of adaptive sampling strategies in complex, real-world applications. Evaluation is conducted through a variety of metrics and methods, and experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithm surpasses a baseline model employing random sampling, achieving faster navigation. This analysis also showcases the versatility of Deep Active Learning by suggesting other possible exploration paths for the robot's visual perception. Finally, the chapter's findings are examined through a multi-domain experiment and we investigate how transferring knowledge from one adaptative system to another can improve performance. A crucial component of intelligent rear-end collision prevention systems is pedestrian detection. Despite notable success in this area, current approaches are limited by their reliance on data from a specific location, which can lead to a high false positive rate in other environments. We propose a novel technique that suppresses false positives based on an object classification task that is performed without supervision, by utilizing a distinct 'box manner' attribute that captures an object's characteristics in an unsupervised manner and defining a metric that measures the difference in object distributions between two different domains in an unsupervised manner through a Gaussian Mixture Model. We test our approach on the widely-used Waymo Pedestrian Dataset and demonstrate its effectiveness through a significant reduction in false positives and an improved detection accuracy in a new environment compared to a baseline model that had been trained on a different dataset. Notably, our approach achieves a high detection accuracy of 64.96% on the entire Waymo Dataset at a false positive rate of 0.5%, surpassing a baseline model that had been trained on a different dataset with a false positive rate of 0.9%. We also visualize the distribution of objects in two different domains to illustrate the effectiveness of our approach through a box re-ranking plot.
