The effectiveness of computational models to predict binding energies depends on the quality of the potential energy surfaces, with recent advances in methods and extensive calculations in astrophysical ice environments leading to improved accuracy.  We introduce the Binding Energy Assessment Platform (BEAP), a database of binding energy distributions, to facilitate comparisons of model performances.  By leveraging existing databases of pre-calculated binding energy distributions, BEAP provides access to over 12000 bindings between molecules and 21 oxygen-containing ice surfaces, as well as ice clusters, water-filled clathrates, and ammonia-based ices at 10K.  Alongside this, BEAP offers ice annealing tools and temperature-dependent binding energy predictions utilizing molecular Monte Carlo simulations, as well as a simplified interface for researchers to assess the performances of their models on the astrophysical timescales relevant to the study of astrochemistry.  Through BEAP, researchers can identify gaps and areas for improvement in their models, supporting model developments that are astrophysically relevant.  We demonstrate the platform's functionality by assessing the performances of two recent water-molecular binding energy models and providing recommendations for their enhancement.  By providing high-quality feedback to model developers, BEAP aims to facilitate discussions, guide future model developments, and ultimately contribute to a more reliable understanding of the complex processes involved in astrochemistry.  We anticipate that BEAP will serve as a resource for astrochemists and molecular physicists to test and validate their models against astrophysically relevant standards, promoting model developments that are astrophysically sound and opening opportunities for applications to various areas within the field of astrochemistry.  We welcome contributions from other groups to BEAP, enabling a collective effort to develop accurate and reliable models to support astrochemical research.  Additionally, we plan to expand on the platform to include more comprehensive databases of binding energy distributions for other types of environments and facilitate comparisons with additional performance metrics in the near future. A multiplicative stochastic process describing geometric growth with a lower bound in a statistical model of a system's density evolution has been developed and tested. It has been applied to analyze two distinct phenomena - the dynamics of a particle's sedimentation and the spreading of a freeze-dried substance disintegrated into powder. The model consists of a geometric progression with a lower bound represented as a gamma-distributed random variable. The shape parameter of this distribution and the lower bound value determine the rate of the geometric progression and the minimum value of the system's density, respectively. The multiplicative process with a lower bound was found to provide a more accurate description of the particle's sedimentation than a standard geometric process. The same approach has been successfully used to simulate the spreading of a powder substance with distinct initial densities. The model's flexibility allows for adjusting its parameters based on experimental observations of the upper bound, namely, the maximum density achieved and the system size. The model's effectiveness has been evaluated by comparing predicted densities with actual ones at different time points. The model's validity has been validated through an analysis of variance, resulting in a p-value of 0.99. The multiplicative process with a lower bound was found to outperform other density evolution models, including the standard multiplicative process and the lagged logistic process. The rates of convergence to the predicted density values were 0.996, 0.090, and 0.079, respectively. Our approach leverages random Clifford circuits, specifically focusing on circuits of a low depth, which makes shadow estimation more efficient both in terms of circuit depth and required qubit usage, compared to traditional shadow estimation methods. Additionally, our approach allows for simpler handling of states that are entangled across multiple qubits, by circumventing the need for circuit rearrangements in response to partial measurements. Furthermore, our approach can achieve improved results under the assumption that the Hamiltonian's effect is limited to a subset of qubits, at a computational cost that scales favorably with the number of affected qubits. Finally, we illustrate the applicability of our approach in estimating the expectation value of a Hamiltonian defined not only by its circuit evolution but also other factors, such as through an experiment with noisy, limited access to two qubits. To address this issue, we investigate various forms of model modification aimed at enhancing the reliability of classification outputs. Our approach, dubbed Sibylvarian, varies from the original SIBYL attack which aimed to identify and exploit weak model predictions by increasing the confidence of the most likely class probability. Besides the original variant, we introduce several new modifications including (1) introducing uniform noise, (2) two-dimensional confidence manipulation (utilizing the relative likelihood of class probabilities and their order), and (3) two-dimensional numerical manipulation (utilizing the relative likelihood of class probabilities and their actual values). These variants display exceptional ability to evade attacks as well as improve the reliability of classification across multiple text-based datasets in multiple English languages. Notably, our model modifications consistently surpass the performance of top-tier adversarial training methods in multiple text classification tasks. Furthermore, we also introduce a new method for determining the most effective threshold for model deployment, which helps to optimize the deployment of our models for high-robustness and high-confidence predictions. Lastly, we introduce a set of challenges for the Adversarial Robustness Challenge at NeurIPS 2022 which focuses on text classification. This paper investigates two techniques for reducing the size of neural machine translation models: quantization learning and knowledge distillation. Using multi-task training, the first approach aims to decrease model weights' variability, whereas the second entails translating a pre-trained high-capacity model into a more compact one. To evaluate their effectiveness in low-resource settings, various benchmark datasets were selected. Our results show that both methods can significantly decrease model sizes without compromising too much accuracy, with distillation outperforming quantization. However, we discovered that both methods struggle with tasks that involve complex relationships, such as translating from English to German. Ultimately, the combination of knowledge utilization and training techniques plays a larger role than the compression method itself in determining compression performance. The findings highlight that there's an opportunity for future research to develop more collaborative strategies between compression methods and knowledge utilization techniques. The experiments' results can be reproduced using https://github.com/fuqiang-kang/Lightweight-NMT/tree/eval-results. Moreover, by utilizing an additional large, 29M weights translation model as an anchor, we could achieve an additional 0.4 BLEU score increase by using an extra 147 weights translation model, which shows that knowledge distillation is more effective than quantization learning in low-resource MT applications. The findings suggest that distillation is more suitable for compressing high-capacity MT models into compact models that can translate tasks with complex relationships, such as translating from English to German. The distillation method's success in this research is consistent with the findings of Alves et al. 2021, which show that pre-training a small MT model on multiple high-capacity models can lead to significantly improved results, a process we call "knowledge distillation for initialization." The distillation techniques outperform the quantization learning method in low-resource settings because it doesn't limit the capacity of the small MT model during training, which allows translation performance to remain high even after compressing models with large variability. Artificial intelligence systems have the potential to cause harm to society, and researchers are pressing for greater transparency in studying these effects. Current methods examining the consequences of AI systems assume that causes of harm correspond to specific features of cases. However, this assumption underpins various techniques such as boosting and ensemble models, which use case data to predict harm, and it does not hold true in general. Furthermore, current methods rely on approximation and data-driven analyses that overlook the role of chance in AI system harm. We contend that understanding the causal nature of harm caused by AI systems offers a promising approach to this challenge. This paper presents a causal framework for modeling harm caused by AI systems, which accounts for both inherent randomness in training data and the role of chance in testing cases. We apply this framework to uncover the inherent causal mechanisms underlying harm caused by AI systems, and our results highlight the need for a more nuanced understanding of AI system harm, differing from current approaches. This causes mechanism discovery can reveal new insights into AI system harm, such as its dependence on underlying control features and how AI systems mitigate or exacerbate their effects. Additionally, our results show that AI systems can cause harm through diverse causal mechanisms and that AI ensemble methods provide protection against these effects. This new line of inquiry may lead the way for future research in AI system harm and causality. Ultimately, our study aims to enhance decision-maker understanding of AI system harm and to make more informed decisions when using AI systems to make critical decisions for people's well-being. We apply our proposed causal analysis to datasets from Mayo Clinic, MIMIC-IV, and Red Cross. These findings illustrate the practical value of this research in the medical and humanitarian sectors. This research was supported by the funding from the The Theai Foundation, a non-profit focused on advancing data AI systems for human benefit. Its mission aligns with our research, which focuses on using AI systems to model the causal effects of harm. This research aims to inform decision-makers in various fields to benefit people in need during critical times. Healthcare, humanitarian work, and other sectors can benefit from this research, which equips AI system developers with a causal perspective on modeling harm. This research also has implications for social sciences, as it demonstrates the use of causal analysis for measuring harm caused by AI systems, which can expand the scope of applications for this concept. Our research introduces zero-shot voice translation, which translates spoken words into target languages without requiring training on specific language pairs. We propose a framework composed of three key components: (1) a multi-lingual acoustic model that can generate speech from written text in multiple languages; (2) a text re-writing model that converts written text from the source language to the target language; and (3) a voice conversion model that synthesizes the target language from the acoustic features generated by the first model, utilizing pre-existing models that don't necessitate further training. We evaluate our approach on a dataset containing spoken passages in English, followed by informal Romanization in Chinese and Japanese and formal transcription in French. Through a user study, we conclude that our method produces voice translation that is indistinguishable from voice-conversed human translations, surpassing existing machine translation speech synthesis and LUescher's zero-shot voice translation. The source code and detailed explanations are available at https://github.com/amanas7/zavt. Our results also lay groundwork for studying the cost of various text re-writing methods, which may be leveraged for developing improved models in the future. We present an updated version of this work at ICASSP 2022, offering rectification techniques to mitigate pronunciation discrepancies in the acoustic models; however, this formulation remains subpar compared to state-of-the-art speech synthesis models. We present another update at Interspeech 2022, which incorporates a self-supervised approach to eliminate the requirement for text re-winding in the target language; however, this formulation is incompatible with zero-shot voice translation. We revisit our research and identify two limitations - the quality of the acoustic models and the compatibility of text re-writing methods. We present an alternative formulation that addresses these concerns, which is compatible with zero-shot voice translation. Specifically, we present an approach that is the combination of the neural speech synthesis, text re-writing, and voice conversion methods. Notably, we present a user study that demonstrates our method is compatible with zero-shot voice translation. We present another update at ICASSP 2023, which is an improvement over the research. The distinguishing characteristic of reacting gas mixtures involves the possession of boundary energies and fluxes whose derivatives are significant in modeling their behaviors. Therefore, treating such systems necessitates the consideration of boundary conditions described by nonlinear differential equations. Building upon the existing theories of heat transfer and reacting gas dynamics, this paper develops a mathematical framework for modeling evolving boundary conditions in systems governed by partial differential equations. Specifically, it derives the necessary conditions for the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the associated nonlinear partial differential equations, including those involving spatial and temporal domains with dynamically changing boundaries. Furthermore, this paper establishes an appropriate maximum principle for the solutions, as well as its applicability to the analysis of free boundary problems in reacting gas dynamics, focusing on the depiction of shrinking, expanding, and stable boundary trajectories. Ultimately, this paper employs the newly formulated theory to explore the behavior of systems protected by a barrier that absorbs and varies in size, as dictated by the laws governing heat transfer and reacting gas dynamics. The work presented here extends the scope of existing theories in these fields, encompassing a broader class of systems with evolving boundary conditions. The authors have also demonstrated the relevance of deriving accurate mathematical frameworks to the practical engineering context of COVID-19 aerosol protection measures. The associated free boundary problem was specifically examined in this study to model the use of face shields as an additional layer of protection against COVID-19 transmission. The results obtained highlight the significance of not only the initial conditions but also the boundary conditions in shaping the final outcomes, as illustrated by the diverse numerical examples presented. The study demonstrates that even small variations in boundary conditions can result in contrasting outcomes, underscoring the need for accurate mathematical representations in determining the system's behavior, especially when the system's dimensions are subject to change. The study presents general theories applicable to a wide range of systems with evolving boundary conditions, as well as a numerical analysis of a specific free boundary problem, demonstrating its practical implications in the context of COVID-9 transmission. As daily energy consumption continues to rise due to growing consumer demands and expanding renewable energy distribution, distributing energy evenly across low voltage networks becomes increasingly crucial. Effective distribution requires accurate and short-term forecasting capabilities, which have been advanced by machine learning techniques. Nevertheless, predicting consumption in the low voltage network presents unique challenges, particularly the need to minimize overall forecasting errors while considering the inherently high variability of daily peak loads. This article addresses these challenges by employing a hybrid forecast fusion approach, which combines both arithmetic and weighted fuzzy voting mechanisms to enhance forecasting accuracy and account for peak load fluctuations. Our study focuses on forecasting consumption in the low voltage network using historical and spatiotemporal data, and employing a persistence forecast as our baseline model for comparison. Our approach involves training a multilinear regression model on individual and aggregated consumption data for both the persistence forecast and forecast fusion scenarios. Our results indicate that forecast fusion significantly surpasses the persistence forecast in terms of mean squared error, and that incorporating daily peak load data as an explanatory variable further improves the model's performance. This research demonstrates that advanced forecasting methods like forecast fusion are particularly valuable for low voltage network consumption forecasting, and that incorporating daily peak load data as an explanatory variable can lead to improved accuracy. Furthermore, our study highlights the potential of using high-resolution data from the distribution system view in favor of reduced availability of lower resolution consumption data from the transmission system view. This paper presents an innovative approach for forecasting consumption in low voltage networks, and demonstrates its practical application in a distribution system setting. Additionally, our results contribute to the development of more reliable models for advanced distribution system management. This research was conducted as part of a larger European research and development initiative, focusing on the Distribution System of the future. This paper presents a subset of this larger project, specifically addressing the challenges and opportunities associated with low voltage network forecasting and control. As such, this content may prove useful to researchers and engineers working on future distribution systems. Furthermore, our study has broader implications for the development of intelligent and adaptive systems for residential energy management, and could potentially be applied to other areas within the broader Energy and Sustainability research context. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, the complexity of spinal anatomy, presence of spinal deformities, and oblique or upright scan positions complicate this task, causing many approaches to struggle. To address these limitations, we introduce an automated system that effectively locates and identifies vertebras in CT scans, even in the presence of complex spinal anatomy and unconventional scan positions. By leveraging the vertebral body's distinctive shape, our approach initializes vertebral position with a fast pipe projection-based method and refines it through a constrained optimization scheme, which utilizes anatomically relevant data to accurately position the vertebral bodies. To enhance convergence speed and robustness, we implement a dynamic graph strategy that dynamically adjusts the optimization focus based on convergence criteria. By integrating a sagittalize strategy, our approach can also automatically detect and correct scan orientation. Through our approach, vertebral bodies can be accurately localized and identified in a wide variety of scan positions and spinal curvatures, which we demonstrate through both numerical simulations and extensive experiments using a dataset consisting of 300 subjects, including pathologies, variations, and imaging modalities. Using an Intel Core i7 processor, our approach identifies and localizes vertebral bodies within an average time of 35ms. To the best of our knowledge, this work presents a groundbreaking, large-scale, and high-speed vertebral localization and identification approach that operates independently of scan position and spinal curvature. Our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of accuracy and efficiency, and has the potential to significantly improve spinal disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. Our approach is available in open-source at https://github.com/yinjiahehkj/Spine_Opt. Our faultless results suggest that an automatic vertebral localization and identification method with high accuracy and efficiency is possible, but may not be feasible in cases with significant vertebral fractures. To address this issue, our approach is modified to identify fractured vertebras by leveraging morphological characteristics, which effectively handles even the most challenging cases. Our approach demonstrates a 100% success rate in identifying vertebral bodies with various levels of fractures, which significantly enhances clinical applications in this area. Our study explores the dynamics of electron collision with a one-dimensional target, under the influence of a laser cavity and a time-varying electromagnetic field. The cavity's phonon and electron polarization fields cause an electron to temporarily experience a force that is opposed by its momentum, leading to an increase in the electron's chances of deflection as it approaches the target. This acute interaction is characterized by a time frame that is comparable to the electromagnetic field's period and the electron travels significant distances relative to the target size, thereby classifying this phenomenon as an example of the light-matter ultrafast coupling regime. An electron collision that occurs near the target resonance is analyzed in depth and the results demonstrate that vacuum fluctuations can either amplify or reduce the resonance's characteristic displacement, depending on the phase and alignment of the electromagnetic field and the target's electron configuration. The studied collision process presents an innovative method for observing coherent radiation and resonant transitions within atoms and molecules. Furthermore, it is proposed that the cavity-generated electron scattering could be utilized to develop a previously unseen type of radiation that is characterized by a time-based correlation higher than 3rd order. This phenomenon, known as "Quantum Soft Coherent Radiation," might hold a unique advantage in generating highly coherent light. The study's conclusions are verified through the analysis of a physical device that incorporates a semiconductor structure, and the experimentally observed electron collision dynamics are compared with predictions made using the Heisenberg equation of motion and the Quantum Monte Carlo Multiparticle dynamics approach. The use of elastic actuators in legged robots has considerable potential to reduce weight, lower energy consumption, and increase mobility. However, developing suitable controllers for these robots poses a significant challenge due to the variable speed of each actuator, which makes traditional position controllers unsuitable for their stiff configurations. To overcome this issue, researchers have made progress in the field of quadruped robots using learning-based approaches to find parameterizations that can accommodate the inherent mobility of these robots, even when their actuators are completely stiffened. By leveraging existing methods for finding parameterizations and optimizing them in simulation environments, researchers have achieved successful control strategies for traversing various gaits generated by these suitable parameterizations. They demonstrated their success through experimental results on an actual elastic-actuator-equipped quadruped robot, revealing that controlling elastic actuators through learned parameterizations can indeed enhance mobility, but may require adjustments to their parameters to transition to stiffer configurations. Notably, transitioning to stiffer configurations using traditional reduction methods can compromise the inherent mobility of these robots, indicating that future optimizations should incorporate both speed schedules and gait transitions to fully harness the benefits of elastic actuators. To further advance this research, researchers aim to expand upon their findings by embedding optimization algorithms directly into the learning-based approaches, which is seen as a promising direction by the research community. A key concept in fashion image retrieval is style, which is crucial for recommending suitable clothing items to users. However, recommending clothes to a user without considering their personal style could be unhelpful. Modifying images by preserving their style can aid in organizing images into style categories, making this task more manageable for retailers. Since defining and collecting large datasets for fashion recommendation is an extensive task, semi-supervised methods can aid in labeling datasets more efficiently. A proposed semi-supervised framework constructs a latent user style feature in the retrieval process and uses this to recommend similar images while preserving the original image's style. The framework uses a cycle consistency loss to ensure retrieved images are of the same style as the query image. The framework can be used to train models in both supervised and semi-supervised scenarios. The framework was tested on datasets from Amazon Fashion Style Retrieval Challenge and our constructed AMZ-FSR-Challenge dataset and showed state-of-the-art performance with a top-1 accuracy of 71.17% and 68.95% respectively. The framework achieved this performance using a small dataset with 5% of the dataset's images while fine-tuning pre-trained models. The framework outperformed other methods with even less data in both experiments. Furthermore, the framework achieved comparable results with more data in both experiments exceeding top results in both datasets. Our approach tackles the issue of using defective optical flow samples in light field images to improve the accuracy of depth estimation. We utilize an iterative cost function, known as the oculation-aware cost builder (OACB), which calculates a shared cost factor for all occluded samples, ensuring their shared optimization. In a iterative process, OACB first predicts a cost factor for non-occluded samples, which are used to estimate the underlying image geometry. These estimates are then used to identify occluded samples and, through mutual information, determine their corresponding optimal correspondences. In a second iteration, the OACB utilizes both occluded and non-occluded samples to estimate the geometry of the scene. We validate our approach with state-of-the-art evaluation results on the standard datasets, 4D and LTPLF. These theories modify GR's action by introducing extra terms, often based on quantities like Ricci curvature or the trace of the Ricci tensor. A new approach based on double field theory is proposed, where modifications of GR's action are tied to specific six-dimensional Weyl invariants. This proposal is compelling as it leverages the rich algebraic structure of T-duality and the theory's fundamental symmetry properties. The results include the intriguing observation that, under certain conditions, these objects may not be tied to each other in four-dimensional spacetimes. Finally, the proposed theory is shown to be tied to theories in higher dimensions, where we recover well-known results and interpret the gravitational memory effect. The potential implications are thus profound and could lead to a significant shift in our understanding of the universe and gravity. In home networks, multiple WiFi access points and repeaters are often used to ensure a strong connection throughout the living space. However, these devices can sometimes cause conflicts with each other, which may result in a decrease in overall WiFi performance. To mitigate this issue, we present a new method, channel load awareness, that is capable of identifying the best channel for each access point or repeater. To achieve this, we suggest conducting periodic surveys across all available WiFi channels to understand activity levels, then utilize the information from these surveys to strategically schedule device activations. This approach allows a substantial decrease in WiFi interference and performance enhancements, most notably when implemented on networks featuring IEEE 802.11b/g/n technology. Similarly, this method demonstrates promising results when applied to networks using IEEE 802.11ac technology. Moreover, this technique operates within the standard framework, is fully compliant with IEEE 802.11k/v specifications, and requires minimal modifications for implementation, consisting essentially of adapting existing surveys and adding a simple activation timing delay to alignment phase, specifically the time it takes to establish a connection with a device. To ensure activation happens within a short timeframe, we present a back-off algorithm that operates locally on each access point or repeater, further ensuring compatibility with IEEE 802.11 standards, specifically IEEE 802.11k's activation timing definition, that specifies that a device needs to activate within a 100ms timeframe, with our approach demonstrating a high likelihood of meeting this requirement in most cases, thus ensuring compatibility with IEEE 802.11k/v technology. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique, we present a simulation study based on a real-world WiFi network, where we present the results of implementing this method across various real-life scenarios, most notably illustrating the effectiveness of channel load awareness in improving WiFi performance via IEEE 802.11k/v technology. This improvement stems from a cross-layer optimization approach that not only operates at the data link layer, where channel load awareness is implemented, by suggesting channel load awareness based on the information from these surveys, but also at the physical layer, where a scheduling technique, the activation timing delay to alignment phase, is employed, thereby reducing interference across all stages of the WiFi network architecture. To ensure the technique is adoptable, we present a clustering method that operates within the standard framework, is fully compliant with IEEE 802.11k/v technology, and requires minimal modifications for implementation, thereby making it a highly effective solution to improving WiFi performance across multiple access points and repeaters.
